newsitem.title: USA: Norfolk Southern launches takeover battle for Conrail.
newsitem.headline: Norfolk Southern launches takeover battle for Conrail.

text.p: Norfolk Southern Corp. launched a full-blown takeover battle Wednesday for Conrail Inc., making a $9 billion offer for its railroad rival and suing in federal court to block an earlier $8.4 billion merger pact between Conrail and CSX Corp.

"This proposal is better on every point than the CSX/Conrail proposal announced last week," Norfolk Southern Chairman David Goode said in a statement announcing his company's bid for Conrail, which had been the subject of speculation on Wall Street.

Philadelphia-based Conrail said in a statement it would review the rival offer, but that it had previously determined a merger with CSX, based in Richmond, Va., rather than Norfolk Southern would be in the company's best interests.

Norfolk Southern said it was beginning a $100 per share cash tender offer for all outstanding common and Series A convertible junior preferred shares of Conrail, beating CSX's bid of $92.50 a share in cash and stock.
Based on the number of outstanding shares of Conrail's stock, the bid is valued at about $9 billion.
Conrail's stock, which did not immediately begin trading when the New York Stock Exchange opened Wednesday, soared when it opened and closed at $95.625, up $11.125.
Norfolk Southern was down 37.5 cents at $94.125 after dropping as low as $91 during the day, in which it also reported 10 percent higher profits for the third quarter.
CSX fell 75 cents to $45.50, and analysts said the firm may be hard pressed to top Norfolk Southern's aggressive bid.

"The Norfolk Southern bid is a very high bid," said analyst Carole Neely of Brown Brothers Harriman. "It's a rich premium and an attractive deal for Conrail shareholders. I don't know if CSX will be able to come up with an all-cash bid."
James Higgins, an anlayst at Donaldson Lufkin & Jenrette, said he thought CSX will.
"I think there's a better than even chance that CSX comes back with a better offer. I think ultimately Norfolk Southern wins," because of a stronger balance sheet, he said.
In a statement released later, CSX Corp. said it believed its offer was better.

"Norfolk Southern's hostile offer comes as no surprise," CSX said in a statement. "It simply does not provide the same long-term value as the strategic CSX-Conrail partnership, which offers Conrail shareholders tax-free equity and the substantial upside potential that only comes from the benefits derived from the merger of CSX and Conrail."
Norfolk Southern, a transportation holding company based in Norfolk, Va., operates a 14,500-mile rail system in 20 states and one Canadian province.

Norfolk Southern said it was prepared to negotiate a merger agreement on substantially the same terms and conditions as CSX's proposed transaction, except that it was offering all cash for Conrail's stock.

"Although we determined that it was appropriate, under the circumstances, to commence our cash tender offer, our strong preference would be to negotiate a merger agreement with you," Goode said in a letter to Conrail's board.

"A combined Norfolk Southern-Conrail will create a more balanced eastern rail system and will do so by increasing, rather than diminishing, competition in the industry," Goode said. He said Norfolk Southern would consider offering some equity in the deal if desired.
In its suit, Norfolk Southern said Conrail had rejected in 1994 its offer of 1.1-to-1 stock-swap merger, and rejected renewed Norfolk Southern advances earlier this month.

The suit said Norfolk Southern's original offer would have been worth $101 per share on the day before the CSX deal was announced, and therefore Conrail must have known it could get a better price for the firm.

The suit sought to block CSX's initial tender offer for 19.9 percent of Conrail's shares, to block a Nov. 14 Conrail shareholders meeting to facilitate the deal, and to win a court declaration that Norfolk Southern could seek to replace Conrail's entire board at the company's annual meeting in May.

"The purpose of the CSX offer is to swiftly transfer effective control over Conrail to CSX in order to lock up the CSX transaction and foreclose the acquisition of Conrail by any competing higher bidder," Norfolk Southern said in the suit, filed in U.S. District Court for Eastern Pennsylvania.
It also accused Conrail of breaking Pennsylvania laws and U.S. securities regulations in its conduct of the CSX deal.

Norfolk Southern said in a separate statement that its net income for the three months ended Sept. 30 grew to $202.3 million, or $1.61 a share, from $183.9 million, or $1.40 a share. Revenues expanded by 2 percent to $1.21 billion from $1.18 billion.
